tone_statements.citation: Kanita Chaimano. 2009. Tonal variation in the Lue dialects of Thailand. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 12(3) [= Special Issue 17]: 1-19. DOI 10.1163/26659077-01203001.
tone_statements.quote: ...presenting an overview of the tonal systems of all Lue dialects in Thailand (including Yong dialects as a subclass of Lue)... The tonal systems of the Lue dialects spoken in Thailand have either five or six tones on smooth syllables. The tone splits and mergers in Column A reveal nine tonal patterns. ... Based on the number of contrastive tones in their tonal systems, Lue dialects can be classified into two groups: Group 1, with five contrastive tones, and Group 2, with six contrastive tones. ... 5-Tone systems(Yong) ... 6-Tone systems (Yong)
tone_statements.locator: p. 2; p. 5 'Comparison of tone numbers'; p. 16 Conclusion; Map 3 legend p. 15
tone_statements.summary: Thai Lue survey incl. Yong villages: 5 or 6 tones on smooth syllables by village (Yong in both groups, Map 3); Chao values per pattern in Fig. 2 (24, 343, 33, 42..); checked tones = allotones.

tone_statements.citation: Kanita Chaimano. 2009. Tone variation of Tai Lue spoken in Thailand. PhD dissertation (Linguistics), Faculty of Graduate Studies, Mahidol University. xiv+219 leaves. Mahidol IR handle 123456789/89229.
tone_statements.quote: The research revealed that Lue dialects are classified into two groups: 5- and 6- tone systems, resulting in 9 patterns of tone system and tone features. Based on the tone split and coalescences in column A the tone system in Lue dialects consists of 5 groups that are A1-2-3-4 (pattern 1 and 6), A1-23-4 (pattern 2, 7/1, 7/2 and 7/3), A1-234 (pattern 3/1, 3/2 and 8/1), A12-34 (pattern 4) and A123-4 (pattern 5/1, 5/2 and 9). It was found that the tone system and tone features of pattern 3/2 are widely distributed in Chiang Mai, Lamphun, Lampang and Nan.
tone_statements.locator: English abstract, p. iv; Yong-specific review sec. 2.2, pp. 28-31
tone_statements.n_tones: 5 or 6 depending on village pattern (9 patterns); Lamphun-area pattern 3/2

tone_statements.citation: ดิศราพร สร้อยญาณะ (Disaraporn Soiyana). 2552 [2009]. การศึกษาวรรณยุกต์ภาษายองเชิงกลสัทศาสตร์: การเปรียบเทียบในบริบทคำพูดเดี่ยวกับคำพูดต่อเนื่องและระหว่างสองรุ่นอายุ [An acoustic study of Yong tones: citation vs connected speech and two generations]. MA thesis (Linguistics), Chulalongkorn University.
tone_statements.quote: จากผลการวิจัยพบว่า ระบบวรรณยุกต์ภาษายองลำพูนมีหน่วยเสียงวรรณยุกต์ทั้งหมด 6 หน่วยเสียง ได้แก่ วรรณยุกต์ที่ 1 กลาง-ขึ้น ปรากฏในช่อง A12 และ DS123 วรรณยุกต์ที่ 2 กลางระดับ ปรากฏในช่อง A34 วรรณยุกต์ที่ 3 ต่ำระดับ ปรากฏในช่อง B123 และ DL123 วรรณยุกต์ที่ 4 กลางค่อนข้างต่ำระดับ ปรากฏในช่อง B4, DL4 และ DS4 วรรณยุกต์ที่ 5 กลาง-ตก ปรากฏในช่อง C123 และวรรณยุกต์ที่ 6 สูง-ตก ปรากฏในช่อง C4
tone_statements.translation: The results show that the tone system of Lamphun Yong has 6 tone phonemes in all, namely tone 1 mid-rising, occurring in boxes A12 and DS123; tone 2 mid level, in box A34; tone 3 low level, in boxes B123 and DL123; tone 4 lower-mid level, in boxes B4, DL4 and DS4; tone 5 mid-falling, in box C123; and tone 6 high-falling, in box C4.
tone_statements.locator: p. 175, ch. 8 §8.1 สรุปผล; same system stated p. 49 §4.1
tone_statements.summary: Six tones (3 level, 3 contour) from Praat F0/semitone measurements of 6 female speakers; contour tones flatten in connected speech; tone sandhi low level + mid level -> second becomes mid-rising.

sources.note: Yong mentioned only in the classification note 'Tai Yong is a dialect of Lue' (the text); the stress discussion concerns Proto-Tai word shape (sesquisyllables), not Yong. Not a Yong description.

sources.citation: Pornsawan Ploykaew. 1985. The phonology of Lue in Chiangrai Province. MA thesis, Mahidol University (held under luuu1242, sister Lue check).
sources.note: Per the luuu1242 summary: p. 46 'Strong stress.. always occurs on a monosyllabic word and on the final syllable of any polysyllabic word.. it is non-phonemic'. This is Lue of Mae Suai (Chiang Rai), not Yong; noted only because Yong is classified as a Lue dialect (Pittayaporn 2009).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Yong language' (en) and 'ภาษายอง' (th), raw wikitext, accessed 2026-09-17.
sources.note: Six tones (from Intajamornrak 2019); nothing on stress; Thai page cites Wangsai 2007.

sources.citation: ปิยาภรณ์ ไชยพันธุ์ (Piyaporn Chaiyaphan). 2567 [2024]. การแปรศัพท์ภาษายอง จังหวัดลำพูน ตามตัวแปรอายุ = Lexical variation of Yong language spoken in Lamphun province by three age groups. MA thesis (Linguistics), Mahidol University, 165 pp. Handle 123456789/91847.
sources.note: Nothing on stress placement. Sec. 2.4 'ระบบเสียงภาษายอง' (pp. 23-26) is a second-hand summary of Yong phonology from Niamnak 1985, Pankhuenkhat 1978, Wangsai 2007 and Soiyana 2009: 21 initials, 9 finals, 18 monophthongs, 6 tones (A12-34, B/C/DL/DS 123-4). The only occurrence of การเน้นเสียง (p. 26) summarises Khanthawong 2010: speech rate and emphasis cause syllable deletion/addition. Full Thai bibliography of Yong phonology work on pp. 124-197.

sources.citation: Intajamornrak, Chommanad. 2019. Tonal variation caused by language contact: a case study of the Yong language. 13th ICLEHI 2019 Osaka, paper 013-012, 9 pp. (Naresuan University).
sources.note: Nothing. Acoustic study of the six Yong tones (Pa Bong Luang, Mae Chan, Chiang Rai; three age groups); 'stress'/'accent' do not occur; only checked vs non-checked syllables. Its reference list names the Yong phonology theses (Neamnark 1985, Pankhuenkhat 1988, Wangsai 2007).

sources.citation: Hartmann, John F. 2008. The Lue language. In Diller, Edmondson & Luo (eds), The Tai-Kadai languages, 254-297. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Nothing on stress in ch. 7 (a full-text search for stress/accent the whole chapter). Discusses Lue of Moeng Yong (Gedney 1969 notes) and Yong of Chiang Mai (Davies 1979) for tone splits; 7.2 Phonology: 'the Tai languages being basically monosyllabic.. the syllable is the unit of tone placement'. Bibliography gives Davies, Somchit 1979 'A comparative study of Yong and Standard Thai', in Theraphan L-Thongkum et al. (eds), 26-48.

sources.note: First-hand tone-box + PRAAT survey: Lue/Yong dialects of Thailand have 5- or 6-tone systems in 9 patterns grouped by column-A splits (A1-2-3-4, A1-23-4, A1-234, A12-34, A123-4); pattern 3/2 is the widespread type in Chiang Mai, Lamphun, Lampang and Nan; sec. 2.2 'Studies of the tone system of the Yong language' summarises Pankhuenkhat 1978 (6 tones, one Pa Sang informant), Davies 1979 (6 tones, Ban Don Chai, Mae Tha), Sarawit 1979 (6 lexical tones + a 7th in dead syllables conditioned by vowel length; Pa Sang and Makhuea Chae) and Niamnak 1985 (eastern A123-4 vs western A12-34 Yong).

sources.citation: Sarawit, Mary E. 1979. Syllabic /m̩/ in two Yoong dialects. In Theraphan L. Thongkum, Vichin Panupong, Pranee Kullavanijaya & M.R. Kalaya Tingsabadh (eds), Studies in Tai and Mon-Khmer phonetics and phonology in honour of Eugénie J.A. Henderson, 163-170. Bangkok: Chulalongkorn University Press.
sources.note: Second-hand (Soiyana 2009 pp. 20-21 with tone box fig. 2.10; Chaimano 2009 pp. 29-30 with table 10): gives the Yong tone system as background to the syllabic-nasal analysis -- six lexical tones (rising, mid level, low level, mid-rising, low-falling, high-falling) plus a seventh high-level tone confined to short checked syllables (DS123), four tone distinctions on checked syllables; Lamphun Yong shares the tonal development of other Northern dialects.
sources.venue: Studies in Tai and Mon-Khmer phonetics and phonology in honour of Eugénie J.A

tone.n_tones: 6 lexical + 1 checked-syllable tone (7 in Sarawit's count)
